articles.body: "My Wi-Fi keeps dropping!" 😩 It's one of the most common help desk tickets, and the usual reply is "restart the router." Sometimes that works. Often it doesn't, and the ticket comes right back. Here's the thing: Windows already keeps a detailed log of every wireless connect and disconnect. One command turns it into a readable report. Let's use it. 🧾 🛠️ Step 1: Generate the report Open Command Prompt or PowerShell as administrator and run: netsh wlan show wlanreport Windows builds an HTML report from roughly the last few days of wireless activity and saves it here: C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WlanReport\wlan-report-latest.html Open it in any browser: start C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WlanReport\wlan-report-latest.html 🔍 Step 2: Read the chart At the top you'll see a timeline o…

articles.title: You cannot review what you never struggled with
articles.excerpt: An engineering director asked who trains junior engineers when nobody is hiring them. The sharpest line in the post is a small one: being good at using AI does not automatically make you good at judgi…
articles.body: An engineering director asked who trains junior engineers when nobody is hiring them. The sharpest line in the post is a small one: being good at using AI does not automatically make you good at judging its output. Judging is a different skill. It comes from the years you spent stuck on a bug until you understood it, and no tool hands you those years. You do not get judgment by watching output go by. You get it by understanding something well enough that the wrong answer looks wrong. Kay P.S. articles.excerpt: In the previous article, we saw how to size and create a Cuckoo Filter. Here we'll see how to do searches, add new values, and remove old ones. For a CF, searches and removals are simple and depend en…
articles.body: In the previous article , we saw how to size and create a Cuckoo Filter. Here we'll see how to do searches, add new values, and remove old ones. Adding a value to a Cuckoo Filter For a CF, searches and removals are simple and depend entirely on the addition logic, so it makes sense to start there. Let's assume we already have a CF with some previously stored fingerprints. We are using 4-bit fingerprints, so a single hex digit (1–9, A-F) is enough. The CF has 8 buckets, each with 2 slots. First, consider the easy case in Figure 11½–18. We want to add GROUCHO ; we calculate its fingerprint (A) and indices (2 and 7), and both buckets have free space, so we can add the fingerprint in either bucket.

articles.body: One of the biggest differences between The Far Side and most other comic strips is that The Far Side doesn’t have a recurring cast of characters. Charles Schulz’s Peanuts , for example, had Charlie Brown, Linus, Lucy, Snoopy, and the rest of the gang, while Jim Davis’ Garfield has Garfield, Odie, Jon, and a handful of other recurring characters. But Gary Larson’s The Far Side , with its non-sequitur, single-panel jokes, didn’t have regular characters, or at least not really .

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

articles.title: Medusa's eye, Halloween fireballs and more: 5 skywatching targets to look out for this spooky season
articles.excerpt: Five spooky skywatching targets perfect for naked eye stargazing this Halloween!
articles.body: The spooky season is officially here! To celebrate, we've put together a list of five Halloween-themed skywatching targets that you can enjoy with nothing but the naked eye or binoculars and, of course, clear skies. Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs. In return, we have imprinted our myths, stories and perceptions upon it, seeing monsters and mythology in the twinkling lights of the stars and assigning sinister aspects to innocent cosmic objects. Many of these ghostly impressions and meanings have survived to the present day. Here are a few of our favorites. The Pleiades open star cluster Don't be fooled by their beauty; the blue-white stars of the Pleiades are dripping in spooky lore.
